titleStmt.title: Optimal Real-Time Task Allocation in Heteregeneous Multi-Core Embedded Systems

analytic.title: Optimal Real-Time Task Allocation in Heteregeneous Multi-Core Embedded Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In response to the increasing complexity of realtime embedded software, driven by the need for intelligent computation in constrained environments, multicore architectures have emerged as a promising solution. The challenge lies in to choose an effective mapping of the real-time tasks to the various computational resources of these embedded boards, while ensuring real-time constraint satisfaction. To address this problem, our approach rests on two pillars. The first is a domainspecific language designed to capture hardware and software characteristics, constraints, and criteria in a clear and unambiguous manner. The second is a solver method based on Satisfiability Modulo Theories solver augmented with a lazy theory to handle real-time aspects. This method allows us to synthesize mappings that respect temporal constraints and optimize specific criteria, such as the power consumption of the embedded board.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent years, the complexity of real-time embedded software has increased significantly, driven by the escalating demand for intelligent computation in embedded systems. This demand has been further fueled by the proliferation of applications that require sophisticated decision-making and data processing capabilities in constrained environments. In response to these evolving requirements, researchers and engineers have turned to multicore architectures as a promising solution. Multicore architectures, which integrate multiple heterogeneous processors on a single chip, offer the potential to significantly increase the computational power and efficiency of embedded systems. However, the effective use of multicore architectures in real-time embedded systems is a significant challenge, especially in environments where different embedded platforms with different technical specifications are deployed. In our lab, we work with a variety of embedded boards (e.g. NXP I.mx8, TI DRA829, Xilinx Zynq ULTRASCALE+, . . . ), each with unique technical characteristics. This diversity adds an additional layer of complexity to the task assignment problem [1]. The allocation problem becomes even more significant when the tasks we want to assign are subject to hard realtime constraints [2]- [4]. The problem we are trying to solve is twofold: first, we need to find a simple way to model all the hardware and software elements and system constraints. Second, we need to find a solution that is efficient enough to be used in our various use cases. In this article, we address this challenge by presenting a comprehensive approach to task allocation in multicore embedded systems. To address this problem, our approach rests on two pillars. The first is a domain-specific language [5] (DSL) designed to capture hardware and software characteristics, constraints, and criteria in a clear and unambiguous manner. This DSL must be simple enough to be used by non-specialists, yet precise enough to capture all the elements necessary to solve the problem. The second is a solver method based on the Satisfiability Modulo Theories solver augmented with a lazy theory [6] to handle real-time aspects. The core of the allocation problem solution is addressed to an SMT solver and the study of the timing constraints of real-time tasks is addressed by the schedulability analysis of the real-time theory solver.

Our method differs from those commonly found in the literature [7], [8] in several ways. First, we propose a method that integrates both a formal modeling of the problem and a solver. Furthermore, our approach, which relies on a lazy SMT solver, produces allocations that are optimal (rather than heuristic) for a wide variety of criteria.

This paper is organized as follows: Sec. II presents the hardware and task models as well as the assignment problem. Sec. III describes the analysis method, including the domainspecific language and the lazy SMT solver extended with realtime theory. Sec. IV provides a practical illustration of our approach. Finally, Sec. V presents a summary and conclusions.

div.head: A. Hardware Model
div.p: The hardware architecture consists of multiple embedded boards (B). Each embedded board has one or more memories (M) characterized by their size, and one or more processors (P) with one or more cores. We consider different cores of the same processor to be strictly identical. However, different processors on the same embedded board can be heterogeneous. Each processor is either used in a bare-metal configuration or has a real-time operating system installed. It is important to note that this configuration mode is associated with one processor and thus all its cores, but an embedded board can manage its processors differently. From the perspective of the real-time task execution assigned to it, the bare-metal or realtime operating system configuration has an impact on the task scheduling policy. In fact, the bare-metal mode implies a nonpreemptive system where tasks are executed sequentially. On the other hand, the RTOS mode allows preemptive scheduling by fixed priority. The strict hardware configuration is known. However, the software configuration, whether bare-metal or RTOS, is an unknown and must be synthesized.

div.head: B. Task Model
div.p: In this article, we consider only classical periodic tasks. Each task τ i is characterized by its period (T i ), priority (P i ), deadline (D i ), and worst-case execution time (C i ). In this article, HP represents the hyperperiod of the entire system, which is defined as the least common multiple of the task periods. Throughout this article, our method calculates the worst-case response time for each task (R i ). If a task's response time is less than or equal to its deadline, then the task is schedulable. If all tasks are schedulable, then the system is considered to be schedulable. Each task is assigned a memory and a core. These allocations are unknown and must be synthesized by the solver.

The hardware architectures we consider in this article are heterogeneous multicore embedded boards with different memory characteristics. Therefore, the choice of allocating a task to a particular memory has a significant impact on the execution time. Thus, the worst-case execution time (WCET) of each task depends on the task's allocation to both memory and processor (not core, since different cores for the same processor are identical). Thus, the WCET of a task τ i as a set of quadruplets (board, memory, processor, C). In this article, we will not detail the techniques used to obtain the different values of C [9], [10]. It should be noted that the worstcase execution time is obtained under maximum perturbations, i.e. it remains an upper bound regardless of task assignment choices and thus interferences.

It is important to note that even though this task model is quite simple, it can take into account precedence constraints with [11] or EDF scheduling policy by considering instances of the tasks. Moreover, the main interest of the proposed method is that the real-time analysis is decoupled from the mapping part, and thus can be extended as needed.

div.head: C. Allocation Model
div.p: The problem we want to solve is the assignment problem, which involves finding an appropriate mapping for each task and configuration for each processor in the system. The solver must determine for each task its allocation, meaning the core on which it is executed and the memory to which it is allocated. Furthermore, the solver must determine the configuration mode of each processor, distinguishing between bare-metal and RTOS. An allocation is considered correct if it satisfies several conditions. First, memory capacities must not be exceeded. Second, all tasks must meet their time constraints (i.e. the system must be schedulable). In addition, certain user-defined constraints, such as collocation and segregation between tasks, must be satisfied. Finally, the solution must also be optimal according to the chosen criterion. The allocation problem is illustrated in Figure 1. The gray areas represent hardware elements, the blue ones represent software components, and the red elements represent the possible mappings to be synthesized. Fig. 1: Task mapping problem.

div.head: A. Method Principle
div.p: The problem we want to solve consists of two distinct parts: an allocation problem and a scheduling problem. Each of these problems has specific and efficient solution methods. The challenge is to effectively integrate these solution methods. In this article, we use an SMT solver to solve the allocation part under constraints, as well as to optimize the criterion. However, the SMT solver alone is not efficient for addressing the study of meeting the timing constraints of real-time tasks.

To study the respect of the temporal constraints of the tasks, we perform a classical schedulability analysis derived from the literature, where the worst-case response time of each task is computed. However, to perform the schedulability analysis, it is essential to know the complete system configuration, which means that the task mapping and the processor configuration ares resolved.

Thus, we have extended an SMT solver with a "lazy" realtime scheduling theory. The principle is as follows: first, the SMT solver solves the allocation problem without considering the real-time constraints of the system. When a solution is found, the scheduling theory calculates the worst-case response times of the tasks and checks that the time constraints are met. If all timing constraints are satisfied, the optimal solution is found; otherwise, the scheduling solver adds information in the form of constraints to the SMT solver. These aim to exclude the current solution and provide information to the SMT solver. Figure 2 depicts the architecture of our solver.

The SMT solvers are efficient at optimizing mappings, and the worst-case response time computation algorithms have low complexity. The challenge lies in the cooperation between the solvers, and more specifically in the ability of the scheduling solver to provide information to the SMT solver. If it only prohibits a non-schedulable assignment, then the SMT solver will enumerate all solutions, and the entire decision process will be too inefficient for use in real-world configurations.

Furthermore, in order to facilitate the utilization of our solver, we have also developed a DSL for the modelling of hardware architectures, tasks, constraints, and criteria. This DSL serves as an entry point to the solver.

div.head: B. Domain Specific Language
div.p: We have defined a DSL for describing real-time multicore embedded architectures. It allows us to easily define the hardware and software characteristics. It also allows us to express knowledge or constraints about allocations, as well as specific constraints such as task collocation or segregation. This language consists of three distinct parts: the definition of the hardware, the definition of the real-time tasks, and the specification of the constraints and the optimization criterion.

Hardware specification: The complete system may consist of several embedded boards. Each board has different memories and processors. Each memory is characterized by its size. Processors have a power index and cores. The power index represents the amount of power the processor consumes when it is active (zero when idle). The listing 3a illustrates the definition of a board with three different memories and two processors, each with multiple cores. Software specification: The software components of the system correspond to the definition of real-time tasks. Each task has a period, a deadline, a WCET, and a memory size. The WCET is specified for each triplet (board, memory, processor) on which its mapping is allowed. The listing 3b shows the definition of the tasks.

Constraints and optimization: In practice, it is very common for users to want to add constraints that are specific to the system they are studying. To accomplish this, we have defined an expression language that allows the specification of various constraints on the system. This expression language includes standard boolean logic operators and allows the use of all elements of the model. In practice, it is often used to define collocation or segregation constraints between tasks mapping, to freeze certain task assignments, or to make decisions about the operating system, for example. It also introduces specific constraints such as modeling processor symmetries (we will return to this notion of symmetry later). Finally, an optimization criterion (maximization or minimization) can be specified. This criterion can be any numerical expression from the expression language. The listing 4 provides an example of user-defined constraints and an optimization criterion.

div.head: C. SMT encoding
div.p: This paragraph explains the SMT encoding to represent this problem. We use an "object" notation to simplify the formulas.

Instances and Sort: The first step in modeling is to define types and instances of those types. For each element of the model (operating system, board, memory, processor, core, task), we create an enumeration (datatype). This allows us to easily type and identify the elements of our model. Listing 5 shows the data types in the model. SMT known functions: Many of the functions we declare are known because they are instantiated in the input DSL. For obvious space reasons, we do not describe their instantiation in detail; they are simply added using SMT asserts and an equality constraint.

All tasks running on a core whose processor is configured in bare-metal mode have the same period. This constraint is closely related to the API we have defined for our various embedded boards. In bare-metal mode, we use a single timer that invokes an execution corresponding to the code sequence of the tasks present on that core. Tasks are therefore executed in order of priority, one after the other.

The possible allocations of tasks to processors and memory are determined by the presence of a WCET value in the DSL of the input problem. In other words, an allocation is possible if and only if there is a corresponding WCET value:

∀ t∈τ (m,p)∈t.wcets t.memory = m ∧ t.core.processor = p (11) User Constraints: Specific user-defined constraints that refer to different elements of the model are simply translated by encoding the expression language we have defined. However, we have added certain global constraints that have special semantics and whose translation into SMT involves both the addition of variables and constraints. One of the most commonly used global constraints is certainly processor symmetry. This constraint indicates that we consider all cores of the given processor to be identical. Therefore, we do not want to explore all possible symmetries of allocations on this processor. To achieve this, we add a constraint that translates a precedence relationship between tasks for the allocation of this processor. This constraint significantly reduces the computation time by halving the state space of possible allocations.

Optimization: The optimization criterion is also a straightforward translation of our expression language into SMT. For example, it allows you to easily express energy minimization or some form of load balancing.

div.head: D. Real-time theory solver
div.p: The real-time theory solver consists of two parts. The first computes the worst-case response time of tasks and checks if they are schedulable. The second is to add constraints to the SMT solver if certain tasks fail to meet their deadlines.

Worst Case Response Time: The calculation of the worstcase response time of tasks depends on the operating system mode of the processor. If the processor is configured in baremetal mode, the response time calculation of the task τ i is simply a calculation by adding the execution times of the tasks in order of priority, where hp(i) is the set of tasks assigned to the same core that have a higher priority than τ i :
div.formula: R i = j∈hp(i) C j + C i(12)
div.p: If the processor configuration mode is RTOS, this means that task scheduling follows a preemptive fixed-priority model. In this case, we use a classical method from the literature [12] to compute the worst-case response time. This calculation consists, for periodic tasks, in finding the fixed point of the sequence given by (13). The only condition is that the core is not overloaded, which is ensured by the SMT constraint (7).
div.formula: R 0 i = C i R n+1 i = R n Ti • C i + j∈hp(i) R n i Tj • C j(13)
div.p: SMT Constraints: If a system does not satisfy its temporal constraints, the real-time theory solver must add constraints to the SMT solver to indicate that the proposed solution is incorrect. However, if the theory solver only prohibits a solution, the SMT solver will enumerate solutions one by one, making the solution very inefficient. Therefore, it is important for the theory solver to provide more constraints for the SMT solver to exclude "classes" of solutions. Thus, if a task τ i does not meet its time constraints, we inform the SMT solver that it is not possible to share this task on this core, memory, and operating system with the other more prioritized tasks. The formulation is as follows, where core i (or j) is the core allocation of the task τ i (or j), and mem i (or j) is the memory allocation (or j):
div.formula: ¬     τ i .core = core i ∧ τ i .memory = mem i j∈hp(i)   τ j .memory = mem j ∧ τ i .core = core i ∧ P j < P i       (14)
div.p: This constraint is well-founded because it relies on the fact that the response time of a task τ i depends only on tasks with higher priority and not on the priority order of those tasks. This constraint generalizes well because it only imposes a priority relationship between the task that does not meet its deadline and the higher priority tasks. Furthermore, it interacts very well with the processor symmetry constraint introduced earlier.

div.head: IV. USE CASE
div.p: In this work we use the Zynq ULTRASCALE+ MPSoC [13] integrated in the ZCU102 evaluation board. The ULTRA-SCALE+ is a heterogeneous platform that includes a complex processing system (quad-core ARM CORTEX-A53, dual-core ARM CORTEX-R5F, ARM Mali-400MP2), programmable logic and a complete memory subsystem (OCM, DDR4 SDRAM). Regarding the processors, we use the CORTEX-A53 [14] and CORTEX-R5F [15]. As for the memory, the board contains 64 KB of B Tightly-Coupled Memory (BTCM), 256 KB of On-Chip Memory (OCM), and 4 GB of SDRAM. Figure 7 shows a simplified view of the MPSoC architecture. The application consists of 6 types of tasks, defined by their memory usage and the instruction issued, and each of them is instantiated 2 times, giving a total of 12 memory intensive synthetic tasks. These tasks traverse a vector that issues a load or a store every cache line size (i.e. 64 bytes), which causes a large amount of interference [16]. Table I summarizes the characteristics of these types of tasks. Tasks can be executed on either CORTEX-A53 or CORTEX-R5F. The A53 can use either the OCM or the SDRAM, while the R5F can use both plus its BTCM. Table II shows the WCET of each task type as a function of the core and memory used. We can see that the R5F execution times in isolation conditions are significantly lower when using OCM than when using SDRAM. For the A53, however, there is no significant difference. Note that for τ 0 , the R5F's use of BTCM or OCM does not reduce the execution time as much as for τ 1 and τ 2 . This is due to the L1D cache, which is able to hold almost the entire vector, thus avoiding higher memory accesses. To calculate the amount of SDRAM interference a task on a core can suffer while working with a specific memory, we measure the on-board WCET of the task while simultaneously running memory intensive tasks on the rest of the cores that target the SDRAM. The resulting values are collected in the Table III. Compared to the Table II, we can see that the A53 suffers from severe interference when targeting either the OCM (e.g. x3.65) or the SDRAM (e.g. x4.90). This is mainly due to the eviction of the shared L2 cache data and the subsequent ACE contention due to data refilling (see Figure 7). The A53 targeting the SDRAM has higher interference due to additional SDRAM contention from the other A53 and R5F cores. The R5F has less interference when targeting the OCM because it is only affected by one R5F core at the RPU switch. It is also less affected than the A53 when targeting SDRAM because there is no other lower memory interference. Note that for τ 0 we have either no interference (BTCM) due to memory and interconnect isolation or very little due to the L1D cache.

div.head: A. Optimal Mapping
div.p: It is important to note that, the R5F processor is in baremetal mode, while the A53 processor has preemptive fixedpriority scheduling. In addition, we have added a constraint that specifies the symmetry of the two processors. Finally, our optimization criterion focuses on minimizing the total power of the board. The solver finds an optimal solution where the power coefficient of the board is 3435.6. Table IV lists the mapping choices and response times. In this example, the SMT solver we are using is Z3 [17]. In the solution table, the second instances of tasks τ i are referred to as τ ib . The computations were performed on an Intel Xeon W-11955M@2.60GHz (single thread) and took 464 ms to find an allocation that satisfies all constraints and 112 seconds to find the optimal solution.

V. CONCLUSIONS In this article, we have presented a tool-assisted method for calculating the mappings of real-time tasks on multicore embedded boards. The entry point of our method is based on a DSL specifically designed for this allocation problem. The solution method is based on an SMT solver augmented with a lazy theory to study the schedulability of the system. The generated solutions guarantee that the tasks respect their time constraints. Furthermore, the produced solution is optimal from the perspective of the criterion specified by the user.

We are currently working on three main improvements. First, we are extending our language and constraints to handle new constraints and criteria. For example, separating the code and data assignments of tasks. Second, we are exploring the possibility of providing parametric WCETs to capture the impact of interferences. In multicore systems, interferences in access to different caches and memory have a significant impact on computation times. The challenge is that the interferences depend on the mapping being synthesized. Finally, we have developed techniques and tools to efficiently perform probabilistic worst-case response time calculations. Therefore, we are also working on integrating WCETs and probabilistic worst-case response times into our tool.
